title: Dependency injection
summary: Dependency injection means giving an object the things it needs (API client, database) from outside instead of creating or fetching them inside. It makes code testable and flexible.
body: **In simple words:** Instead of `let api = APIClient()` inside your view model, you pass `api` in through `init`. In production you pass the real client; in tests you pass a fake that returns fixed data.
**Real-life analogy:** A chef who is handed ingredients can cook anywhere. A chef who must go to one specific shop for every ingredient cannot work if that shop is closed.
**Types:** **Initializer injection** (best: explicit, checked by compiler). Property injection (set after init; used for storyboards). Method injection (pass per call).
**Composition root:** one place (the app target / app start) creates the real implementations and wires them together. Feature modules only see protocols.
**At scale:** group dependencies in a per-feature `Dependencies` struct to avoid huge inits; containers like Factory/Swinject, or `swift-dependencies`; SwiftUI `@Environment` for view-level services.
**Singletons:** acceptable for truly global, stateless things, but hide them behind a protocol so tests can replace them.
keyPoints: Pass dependencies in; prefer initializer injection.
Depend on protocols or structs of closures so tests can use fakes.
Wire real implementations in one composition root.
Containers trade compile-time safety for convenience (missing registration = runtime crash).
DI enables unit tests without network, database or time.

code.caption: Struct-of-closures client (easy to fake)

mistakes: Service locators used everywhere, hiding what each type really needs.
followups: **How do you test time-based code?** Inject a clock (`any Clock<Duration>`) and advance it in tests.
**DI container or manual DI?** Manual for small/medium apps; containers when the graph is large, with tests that verify all registrations.
